questions.q: Which of the following molecules can participate in hydrogen bonding as a hydrogen bond donor? (i) CH₄ (ii) NH₃ (iii) HCl (iv) CH₃OH. Select all that apply.
questions.a: Correct: (ii) NH₃ and (iv) CH₃OH. Hydrogen bond donors require H bonded directly to N, O, or F. NH₃ has N–H bonds; CH₃OH has O–H bond. CH₄ has C–H (C not electronegative enough); HCl has H–Cl (Cl is electronegative but larger size reduces charge density, making H-bonding very weak – not considered significant in Class 11). A wrong answer reveals confusion between electronegativity alone vs. the combined requirement of high electronegativity AND small atomic size (high charge density).

questions.q: Explain why HF forms stronger hydrogen bonds than H₂O, yet water has a higher boiling point (100°C vs 19.5°C).
questions.a: Correct: F is more electronegative than O, so the H–F bond is more polar, giving stronger individual H-bonds in HF. However, each H₂O molecule can form up to four H-bonds (two as donor via two H atoms, two as acceptor via two lone pairs on O), creating an extensive 3D network. HF can form only two H-bonds per molecule (one H as donor, three lone pairs on F but steric hindrance limits acceptance). The cooperative network in water requires more energy to break, raising its boiling point. A wrong answer focusing only on bond polarity reveals failure to consider the number of H-bonds per molecule and network dimensionality.

questions.q: Arrange the following in order of increasing boiling point: CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, HF. Justify your answer using intermolecular forces.
questions.a: Correct order: CH₄ (–161°C) < NH₃ (–33°C) < HF (19.5°C) < H₂O (100°C). CH₄ has only weak London forces. NH₃, HF, H₂O have H-bonding. Among H-bonded species: NH₃ forms weaker H-bonds (N less electronegative than O/F) and each N has only one lone pair. HF has strong H-bonds but limited network (linear chains). H₂O forms the most extensive 3D H-bond network (two donors + two acceptors). A wrong order reveals inability to weigh both H-bond strength AND number of H-bonds per molecule.

questions.q: Compare the density of ice and liquid water at 0°C. Explain the structural reason using hydrogen bonding geometry.
questions.a: Correct: Ice (0.917 g cm⁻³) is less dense than liquid water (0.9998 g cm⁻³ at 0°C). In ice, each water molecule is tetrahedrally H-bonded to four neighbors, creating an open hexagonal crystalline structure with large empty spaces. On melting, some H-bonds break, molecules move closer, and density increases. This is anomalous – most substances are denser as solids. A wrong answer (e.g., ice denser) reveals misunderstanding of H-bond directionality and tetrahedral geometry creating voids.

questions.q: A student claims: "Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) has a higher boiling point than water because it has a larger molar mass (46 vs 18 g mol⁻¹) and also forms hydrogen bonds." Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: Claim is false. Ethanol boils at 78°C, water at 100°C. While both H-bond, water forms a 3D network (two H-donors, two lone-pair acceptors per molecule). Ethanol has only one O–H group (one donor, two acceptors) and a bulky nonpolar ethyl group that disrupts the H-bond network. London forces from the ethyl group are insufficient to compensate. The student incorrectly assumes molar mass dominates over H-bond network extent. This reveals confusion between additive London forces and cooperative H-bond networking.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using household materials to demonstrate that hydrogen bonding affects surface tension. Describe procedure, observation, and explanation.
questions.a: Good answer: Float a clean steel needle on water in a bowl (surface tension supports it). Add a drop of detergent (disrupts H-bonding at surface). Needle sinks. Explanation: Water's high surface tension (72 mN m⁻¹) arises from strong cohesive H-bonding pulling surface molecules inward. Detergent molecules insert between water molecules, breaking H-bonds and lowering surface tension. Poor answer (e.g., "mix oil and water") shows confusion between surface tension and immiscibility, or inability to link molecular H-bonding to macroscopic property.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Hydrogen bonding is a special type of dipole-dipole ______ that occurs between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F) and another electronegative atom bearing a lone pair of electrons.
Fill in the blank: Start with a familiar ______: why does water boil at 100°C while H₂S (heavier molecule) boils at –60°C?
What is Hydrogen bonding? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Hydrogen bonding is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction that occurs between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F) and another electronegative atom bearing a lone pair of electrons.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: End with the key generalization: H-bonding creates a ______D network in water, explaining its high boiling point, density anomaly (ice floats), and high surface tension.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Hydrogen bonding?
questions.a: Students believe any molecule with H and an electronegative atom (like Cl, S) forms hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify molecules capable of hydrogen bonding, distinguish between intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding, and explain anomalous physical properties (boiling point, density, viscosity) of substances like H₂O, HF, and NH₃ using hydrogen bonding concepts.
